summary: 11b concludes the baraita about which structures require a mezuza: gatehouses, porticos and balconies are excluded (not for dwelling); bathrooms, tanneries, bathhouses and mikvaot are excluded (not designed for honor); Temple Mount, chambers and courtyards are excluded (sacred, not mundane) - a decisive refutation of Rav Yehuda. A second tannaitic dispute lists six (actually seven) gate types that are exempt, including the Median gate (a domed arch), subject to a dispute between R. Meir and the Rabbis about whether theoretical enlargement completes a measurement. The daf then establishes that synagogue, woman's house and partners' house all require a mezuza and are susceptible to tzaraat; the mezuza verse's leftover restrictive sense is redeployed by Rava to fix the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway, while the tzaraat verse's leftover restrictive sense is redeployed to a separate moral - a stingy homeowner who hoards his vessels and falsely denies owning them will be exposed by God through tzaraat, excluding one who lends his vessels to others. A further baraita contradicting the synagogue-tzaraat ruling draws two resolutions - tanna attribution, then a caretaker's-residence distinction - before a third alternative begins and is cut off mid-sentence at the daf's physical end, left unresolved.

display.title: Concluding the baraita - three reasons for exemption
display.oneLine: The baraita concludes with three categories of mezuza-exempt structures: not-for-dwelling, not-for-honor, and sacred but non-residential.
display.shortSummary: The baraita lists three grounds for mezuza exemption. First: gatehouse, portico, and balcony are exempt because they are not designated as dwellings - people pass through or rest there but do not live there. Second: bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, and mikveh are exempt because they lack the quality of honor (kavod) that a mezuza requires - undressing or undignified work makes the space inappropriate for the sacred text. Third: Temple Mount, Temple chambers and courtyards are exempt because they are sacred but not mundane residences. This third category is a definitive refutation of Rav Yehuda's position that the Parhedrin chamber mezuza was a Torah obligation.
display.whats: The baraita that was cut off at the end of 11a now concludes on 11b. Three exclusion principles from the word 'house': (1) not designated for dwelling (gatehouse, portico, balcony); (2) not designed for honor (bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, mikveh); (3) sacred-but-not-residential (Temple precinct) - stated on vilnaLines 8-9 after the hypothetical extension on vilnaLine 7. The third is sealed as the decisive refutation of Rav Yehuda's claim that the Parhedrin chamber required a Torah-level mezuza by the word תיובתא opening vilnaLine 10.
display.hint: The Gemara builds its list of exemptions by repeated application of the same verse - each time drawing a different inference from the word 'house.' The sacred/mundane distinction is the most unexpected: one might think a holier space deserves a mezuza, but sanctity and residential character are different categories.

learning.learnerQuestion: Why would the Temple Mount - the holiest place in the world - be exempt from mezuza? Shouldn't holier places have more, not fewer, religious obligations?
learning.coreTension: Mezuza marks a domestic residence, not a sacred site. The Temple Mount is sacred (kodesh) not residential (dirat adam). These are different halakhic categories: domestic sanctity vs. Temple sanctity. The mezuza belongs in the first category, not the second.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara identifies three distinct reasons for exemption (not-dwelling, not-honor, not-mundane-residential), showing that mezuza obligation is multi-conditional: a space must be (1) used as a dwelling, (2) used with dignity, and (3) not a sacred precinct reserved for Temple service.
learning.resolution: The three-part framework is established. The Temple Mount/chamber exemption definitively answers the question of the Parhedrin chamber: since the whole Temple is categorically exempt, the Parhedrin chamber's mezuza must be rabbinic only. This confirms the Sages' position against Rav Yehuda.

takeaway.text: A mezuza marks a human home, not divine space. The Temple's exemption from mezuza reveals that mezuza is a domestic institution - it belongs where people live, not where God is formally served. This is why the KG's personal chamber required a special decree: the Temple setting normally exempts everything there from mezuza.

reasoningPattern.notes: Mezuza requires three positive conditions (dwelling, honor, mundane-residential). The baraita systematically eliminates structures that fail one of these three tests, building a complete framework for mezuza eligibility.

learning.ahaMoment: The Temple exemption is the most counterintuitive: holier = less mezuza obligation, not more. This reveals a deep halakhic principle: domestic law and Temple law operate in different categories. The mezuza tracks the human household, not divine service.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may confuse 'exempt from mezuza' with 'less holy' or 'not important.' The Temple's exemption has nothing to do with its holiness - it is exempt because it is a sacred precinct, not a domestic residence, and mezuza is specifically a domestic institution.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three exemptions, three reasons: (1) Gatehouse - you pass through, not live in. (2) Bathroom - undressing, no kavod. (3) Temple Mount - sacred but not your house. The third is the knockout punch against Rav Yehuda's Torah-level claim.

argumentFlow.label: Exemption 1: not-dwelling structures
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: Gatehouse, portico, and balcony are exempt from mezuza because they are not designated as dwellings. People may pass through or rest there, but these spaces are not someone's home.

sourceRefs.note: First exemption category: structures not used as dwellings

argumentFlow.label: Exemption 2: structures lacking honor
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: Bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, and mikveh are exempt because these spaces lack the quality of kavod (honor/dignity) that makes a space appropriate for a mezuza containing the Shema.

sourceRefs.note: Second exemption category: undignified spaces

argumentFlow.label: Exemption 3: Temple precinct - refutation of Rav Yehuda
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: The hypothetical extension on vilnaLine 7 asks whether the Temple Mount, chambers and courtyards should also be included. The actual exclusion is stated on vilnaLines 8-9: 'house' implies a mundane (non-sacred) structure, so sacred precincts are excluded. This exclusion is sealed as the decisive refutation of Rav Yehuda by the word תיובתא opening vilnaLine 10: since the whole Temple precinct is categorically exempt, the Parhedrin chamber's mezuza must be only rabbinic.

sourceRefs.note: Hypothetical extension to Temple Mount and chambers - not yet resolved
The actual exclusion: 'house' implies mundane, excluding sacred precincts
Opening word תיובתא seals this exclusion as the decisive refutation of Rav Yehuda's Torah-level claim

misconceptions.misconception: The Temple's exemption from mezuza means it is less holy than an ordinary home.
misconceptions.correction: The opposite: the Temple is exempt because it is too sacred to be classified as an ordinary domestic residence. Mezuza is a domestic institution that marks human habitation, not divine service.

Temple Mount with 'no mezuza' label - counterintuitive holiness/obligation relationship

quizSeeds.question: Why is a bathroom exempt from mezuza even though people regularly use it?
quizSeeds.answer: Because it lacks the quality of kavod (honor/dignity) required for a mezuza. Undressing and using the bathroom makes the space inappropriate for a sacred text containing the Shema.

quizSeeds.question: How does the baraita's third exemption category (Temple Mount and chambers) refute Rav Yehuda?
quizSeeds.answer: Since the entire Temple precinct is categorically exempt from mezuza as sacred (not residential) space, the Parhedrin chamber's mezuza cannot be a Torah obligation. It must be only a rabbinic decree - confirming the Sages' position.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The three conditions for mezuza obligation: dwelling, honor, mundane residential
Why sacred Temple space is categorically different from domestic space

display.title: Six gates exempt - the Median gate and the dome dispute
display.oneLine: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda lists six (actually seven) gate types exempt from mezuza, with the Median domed-arch gate generating a dispute between R. Meir and the Rabbis about whether theoretical enlargement counts.
display.shortSummary: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda states six types of gates are exempt from mezuza. But his list actually contains seven - the fifth is the Median gate (sha'ar Madi), which is a domed arch without proper doorposts. Rava explains the Median gate involves a tannaitic dispute: R. Meir holds that if you could theoretically carve the arch to create proper doorposts of the required dimension, treat it as if they already exist (chokkein lehashlem - theoretical completion). The Rabbis disagree: you cannot use theoretical future action to fulfill present requirements.
display.whats: VilnaLine 10 opens with the word תיובתא, sealing the refutation of Rav Yehuda that concludes the previous sugya's exclusion of the Temple precinct, before this sugya's own content begins mid-line. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda claims six gates are exempt, but actually lists seven - the fifth is the Median gate (a domed arch with no doorposts). Rava explains: the Median gate is a tannaitic dispute between R. Meir (theoretical enlargement counts) and the Rabbis (it does not). VilnaLines 23-24 state the dispute's actual positions: R. Meir holds chokkein lehashlem (one carves to complete), and the Rabbis hold ein chokkein lehashlem (one does not) - this sugya's content runs through line 24, where the next sugya's baraita ('תנו רבנן: בית...') begins.
display.hint: Chokkein lehashlem (theoretical completion) is one of R. Meir's distinctive rulings: if a space could be enlarged to meet the required measurement, treat it as if it already meets it. The Rabbis disagree. This principle appears in multiple halakhic contexts wherever minimum dimensions matter.

learning.learnerQuestion: What makes a gate a real 'gate' for mezuza purposes? And what is the Median gate's architectural problem?
learning.coreTension: A domed arch (like the Median gate) has no doorposts - it is a curved opening rather than a rectangular frame with sideposts. The question is whether the curved stone, which could theoretically be carved to create proper doorposts, counts as having doorposts now. R. Meir says yes; the Rabbis say no.
learning.coreMove: R. Meir's chokkein lehashlem principle: potential or theoretical compliance with a dimensional requirement is treated as actual compliance. This is a legal fiction that the Rabbis reject - for them, what exists currently matters, not what could theoretically be made.
learning.resolution: The dispute is unresolved - both R. Meir's and the Rabbis' positions are preserved. In practice, the Median gate is treated as exempt by most (since the Rabbis are the majority view against R. Meir on this).

takeaway.text: Halakhic dimensional requirements are assessed based on the current reality, not on what could theoretically be made. R. Meir's dissenting position (theoretical completion counts) is a significant minority view preserved for its principled basis.

reasoningPattern.notes: R. Meir applies a consistent principle across multiple contexts: theoretical compliance with a minimum satisfies the current requirement. The Rabbis consistently reject this because they require actual current compliance.

learning.ahaMoment: The Median gate illustrates that architectural form (arch vs. rectangle) has direct halakhic consequences. A domed entry that is visually impressive may have no mezuza obligation at all because it lacks the physical structure (doorposts) that mezuza requires.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the dispute is about measuring existing stones. It is about a theoretical action: could you carve the dome to create doorposts? R. Meir says that possibility changes the current status; the Rabbis say only actual existing doorposts matter.
learning.memoryAnchor: Six gates, but really seven. The fifth is the Median dome - no doorposts, can't put a mezuza. R. Meir: carve it and it's as if it already has doorposts. Rabbis: not yet built = not yet counted.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda: six gate types exempt
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: VilnaLine 10 opens with תיובתא - the refutation of Rav Yehuda concluding the prior sugya's third exclusion - before this sugya's own statement begins on the same line: six types of gates are exempt from mezuza. The list is given - but a careful count shows seven types.

sourceRefs.note: Opens with תיובתא (shared boundary with the prior sugya), then the six (actually seven) gate types

argumentFlow.label: Why does the list have seven items, not six?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rava explains: the Median gate (sha'ar Madi, a domed arch) is a tannaitic dispute. When the list says 'six,' it excludes the Median gate because it is subject to R. Meir vs. Rabbis disagreement - one tanna exempts it, the other does not.

sourceRefs.note: Rava's explanation of the six vs. seven discrepancy

argumentFlow.label: R. Meir vs. Rabbis: chokkein lehashlem
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Meir / Rabbis
argumentFlow.text: The Median gate is a domed arch with no doorposts. R. Meir: if you could theoretically carve the arch to create standard doorposts of the required dimension, it is as if they already exist (chokkein lehashlem). The Rabbis: theoretical future action does not create present halakhic status.

sourceRefs.note: R. Meir holds chokkein lehashlem
The Rabbis hold ein chokkein lehashlem; this shared line then begins the next sugya's baraita

misconceptions.misconception: The Median gate is exempt because it is foreign/non-Jewish architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The exemption (for the Rabbis) is purely structural: the arch has no doorposts to attach a mezuza to. Whether it is Median, Roman, or any other style is irrelevant - the physical structure determines the obligation.

Carving diagram: how the dome could theoretically be carved to create doorposts (R. Meir's position)

quizSeeds.question: Why is the Median gate (sha'ar haMadi) unique among exempt gate types?
quizSeeds.answer: Because it is the only type that is a tannaitic dispute. All other exempt gate types are agreed upon; the Median gate (a domed arch with no doorposts) is exempt according to the Rabbis but R. Meir holds it is obligated via his chokkein lehashlem principle.

quizSeeds.question: What is R. Meir's chokkein lehashlem principle?
quizSeeds.answer: If a space could theoretically be enlarged or carved to meet a required minimum measurement, treat it as if it already meets that measurement. Applied to the Median gate: since the arch could be carved to create proper doorposts, R. Meir treats it as already having them.

R. Meir's general approach of applying theoretical-completion reasoning to halakhic minima
Basic architectural distinction between arched/domed and rectangular doorways

display.title: Synagogue, woman's house and partners' house: mezuza and tzaraat
display.oneLine: Two parallel baraitot establish that synagogues, women's houses, and partners' houses both require a mezuza and are susceptible to tzaraat (house-plague).
display.shortSummary: Two baraitot teach in parallel: the same three categories of houses (synagogue, woman's house, partners' house) are obligated in mezuza AND susceptible to tzaraat. In the mezuza baraita, the word 'your house' (masculine singular) might seem to exclude women and partners; the universal reward verse shows it doesn't, and Rava redeploys the leftover restrictive sense to fix the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway. In the tzaraat baraita, the word 'his house' might similarly seem to exclude women and partners; the inclusive verse shows it doesn't, and the leftover restrictive sense is redeployed to a different moral: a stingy owner who hoards his vessels and denies owning them will be exposed by God through tzaraat, excluding one who lends his vessels to others.
display.whats: Two parallel baraitot teach the same lesson about three categories of houses - synagogue, woman's house and partners' house. Both are obligated in mezuza and both can receive tzaraat. In each case the relevant word (‘your house’ for mezuza, ‘his house’ for tzaraat) might seem to exclude women and partners, but it doesn't: for mezuza, the universal reward verse proves inclusion; for tzaraat, the verse ‘in a house of the land of your possession’ proves inclusion. Each verse's leftover restrictive sense is then redeployed to a separate teaching: Rava uses ‘your house’ to fix the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway, while ‘his house’ is redeployed to teach that a stingy owner who hoards his vessels and denies owning them will be exposed by God through tzaraat when forced to empty his house - excluding one who lends his vessels to others.
display.hint: Why do 'your house' and 'his house' each get overridden by an inclusive verse, and what does their leftover restrictive sense end up teaching instead - mezuza placement on the right side of the doorway, and which homeowner tzaraat actually exposes?

learning.learnerQuestion: If 'your house' and 'his house' might each exclude a synagogue, a woman's house, or a partners' house from mezuza and tzaraat, how does the Gemara justify including them anyway - and what does each excluding word end up teaching instead?
learning.coreTension: The word 'your house' (beitecha, masculine singular) could exclude a synagogue, a woman's house, and a partners' house from mezuza; the parallel word 'his house' (lo) in the tzaraat verse could exclude the same three categories from tzaraat. The Gemara needs a textual basis to include all three in both laws without discarding either word's exclusionary force entirely.
learning.coreMove: For mezuza, the Gemara points to the universal reward verse to include all three categories, then Rava redirects 'your house''s leftover exclusionary force to teach the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway. For tzaraat, the Gemara points to the inclusive verse 'in a house of the land of your possession' to include all three categories, then redirects 'his house''s leftover exclusionary force to a different moral: it identifies the stingy owner who hoards his vessels and denies owning them as the one tzaraat exposes, excluding the generous lender.
learning.resolution: Synagogue, woman's house, and partners' house are all obligated in mezuza and susceptible to tzaraat, because inclusive verses override the narrow readings of 'your house' and 'his house.' The leftover exclusionary sense of each phrase is reassigned to its own separate teaching: 'your house' to the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway, and 'his house' to the moral that a stingy, lying homeowner who refuses to lend his vessels will be exposed by tzaraat, while one who lends his vessels is excluded.

takeaway.text: When an inclusive verse exhausts the exclusionary force of a phrase, the Gemara does not discard the leftover restrictive sense - it redeploys that leftover meaning for an unrelated halakhic or moral detail. Here this happens twice: once for mezuza placement, and once for identifying who tzaraat exposes.

reasoningPattern.notes: Twice in this sugya, a word that seems to exclude synagogues/women/partners ('your house' for mezuza, 'his house' for tzaraat) is first neutralized by an inclusive verse, then its leftover restrictive sense is redirected to a separate teaching: mezuza placement on the right side of the doorway, and the stingy homeowner exposed by tzaraat - a classic double-duty derash pattern.

learning.ahaMoment: Woman's house and partners' house require both mezuza and are susceptible to tzaraat even though 'your house'/'his house' might suggest only a sole male owner's house is included. The Gemara uses inclusive verses to include them in both laws, then recycles each verse's exclusionary language for a separate lesson: mezuza's placement, and the stingy owner tzaraat exposes.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may expect the exclusionary reading of 'your house'/'his house' to simply disappear once the Gemara includes synagogues, women, and partners in both laws. Instead, the Gemara's derash style reassigns each leftover restrictive sense to a new topic entirely - mezuza placement, and the stingy homeowner exposed by tzaraat - rather than treating it as resolved and discarded.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three categories, same rule twice: mezuza AND tzaraat. Synagogue, woman's house, partners' house - all in, all out together. 'Your house' and 'his house' each seem to exclude them, but inclusive verses include them - and each leftover exclusion is recycled: one to fix the mezuza on the right side of the doorway, the other to expose the stingy homeowner who won't lend his vessels.

argumentFlow.label: Baraita: three house categories require mezuza
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: Three types of houses require a mezuza despite the word 'your house' (beitecha) possibly suggesting exclusion: a synagogue, a woman's house, and a partners' house. The universal reward verse shows that women and partners are included in the obligation.

sourceRefs.note: First baraita: mezuza obligation for three house types

argumentFlow.label: The universal reward verse includes women and partners
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara rejects the proposed mezuza exclusion because the reward verse promises long life to all who observe the commandment. Women and partners therefore remain included; this proof is specific to mezuza and is not the later tzaraat derivation.

sourceRefs.note: The universal mezuza reward verse includes women and partners

argumentFlow.label: What does the leftover exclusionary sense of 'your house' teach, if not exclusion?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: If 'your house' does not exclude synagogues, women, or partners from mezuza, what does its restrictive language teach instead? Rava explains that beitecha is redeployed to fix the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway, matching the direction one enters with the right foot first.

sourceRefs.note: Rava redirects the leftover restrictive sense to the mezuza's placement on the right side of the doorway

argumentFlow.label: Parallel baraita: the same three categories, now for tzaraat
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: A second, related baraita teaches that a synagogue, a partners' house, and a woman's house all become impure with tzaraat like other houses. The Gemara again asks why this needs stating, and answers: lest you say the verse ‘the one whom the house is his’ (lo) excludes a house belonging to a woman or to partners.

sourceRefs.note: Second baraita: tzaraat susceptibility for the same three house types, raising the 'lo' exclusion concern

argumentFlow.label: What does the leftover exclusionary sense of 'his house' teach, if not exclusion?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: VilnaLine 33 only reaches the point of introducing the inclusive verse ('אמר קרא'); the verse itself - 'in a house of the land of your possession' (vilnaLine 34) - shows tzaraat applies to all houses, so women's and partners' houses are not excluded. If 'his house' (lo) does not exclude them, what does its restrictive language teach instead? VilnaLines 34-35 describe the stingy homeowner who refuses to lend his vessels and falsely denies owning them, whom God exposes through tzaraat. The opening words of vilnaLine 36 complete only this teaching by excluding one who lends his vessels to others; the new synagogue contradiction that follows on the same line belongs to the next sugya.

sourceRefs.note: Introduces the inclusive verse ('אמר קרא') but does not yet state it
The inclusive verse itself: 'in a house of the land of your possession'
Only the opening words, פרט למשאיל כליו לאחרים, complete the stingy-homeowner teaching by excluding one who lends; the synagogue contradiction later on this shared line belongs to s04

misconceptions.misconception: A synagogue gets tzaraat as a punishment for sins committed there.
misconceptions.correction: Tzaraat of a house is a divine signal to its owner, not a punishment for the building. This sugya establishes that a synagogue, like a woman's house and a partners' house, is included in tzaraat law because an inclusive verse overrides the narrow reading of 'his house.' The synagogue's sacred character is irrelevant to tzaraat's application.

misconceptions.misconception: The word 'his house' (lo) in the tzaraat verse is simply dropped once the Gemara includes women's and partners' houses.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara never treats 'his house' as discarded. Its leftover restrictive sense is redeployed to a specific moral: a homeowner who keeps his vessels only to himself, refuses to lend them, and falsely denies owning them is the one God exposes through tzaraat when his house must be emptied. One who lends his vessels to others is excluded from this exposure - 'his house' is not about ownership exclusion at all, but about the stingy owner's comeuppance.

visualizableElements.item: Mezuza affixed to the right side of a doorway - the direction one enters with the right foot first
Parallel columns: mezuza baraita / tzaraat baraita - same structure, same categories
A homeowner forced to empty his house of hoarded vessels in public, exposing his refusal to lend them - the moral the tzaraat verse's exclusionary word is redeployed to teach

quizSeeds.question: Why is a woman's house obligated in mezuza if the Torah says 'your house'?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the reward verse for mezuza observance applies universally to all who observe it, including women. 'Your house' cannot be read to exclude women from the obligation - the inclusive reward language proves this.

quizSeeds.question: Once the reward verse shows 'your house' includes synagogues, women's houses, and partners' houses, what does the word's leftover exclusionary sense end up teaching?
quizSeeds.answer: Rava redirects it to a mezuza-placement teaching: the mezuza is fixed on the right side of the doorway, matching the direction one enters with the right foot first.

quizSeeds.question: The tzaraat verse uses the word 'his house' (lo), which might exclude women's and partners' houses from tzaraat. Once the Gemara proves they are included, what does 'his house' end up teaching instead?
quizSeeds.answer: It reveals which kind of owner tzaraat exposes: one who dedicates his house to himself alone, refuses to lend his vessels, and falsely denies owning them. God exposes him by forcing his house to be emptied of its hoarded contents - excluding one who lends his vessels to others.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The basic laws of tzaraat (house-plague) from Leviticus 14
That tzaraat requires a personal owner to receive the divine warning
The structure of parallel baraitot sharing the same reasoning across different laws

display.title: Does a synagogue get tzaraat? A contradiction, partly resolved
display.oneLine: The contradiction between two baraitot - one saying synagogues get tzaraat, the other saying they do not - is addressed by two resolutions, then a third begins and is cut off mid-sentence at the end of the daf.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara faces a direct contradiction: one baraita says synagogues are susceptible to tzaraat; another says they are not (since they are not designated for one specific person). Two resolutions are given in full. First: the first baraita is R. Meir, the second is the Rabbis. Second (both baraitot are the Rabbis): a synagogue with a caretaker's residence attached is included, one without is excluded. A third alternative then begins - proposing that both baraitot concern synagogues without a caretaker's residence, distinguished by some other factor - but the Gemara's text breaks off mid-sentence (the fragment 'and the...') at the physical end of the daf, before stating what that factor is.
display.whats: A second baraita contradicts the first: it says synagogues and study halls do NOT get tzaraat (they are not designated for one specific person). The Gemara offers two completed resolutions: (1) First baraita = R. Meir, second = Rabbis. (2) Both baraitot are the Rabbis: a synagogue with a caretaker's residence attached is included, one without a caretaker's residence is excluded. A third resolution then opens - suggesting both baraitot actually concern synagogues WITHOUT a caretaker's residence, divided by some other criterion - but the daf ends before that criterion is stated, leaving the third resolution unresolved.
display.hint: Which of the three attempted resolutions does the Gemara actually finish stating before the daf physically ends?

learning.learnerQuestion: Can a synagogue ever get tzaraat? The two baraitot seem to give opposite answers.
learning.coreTension: Tzaraat requires a designated owner ('his house'). A synagogue is communally owned. When is communal ownership specific enough to count as personal ownership for tzaraat? Each resolution identifies a different principle for when communal ownership is sufficient - and the daf ends before the discussion is complete.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara does not simply declare one baraita correct and the other wrong. It finds conditions under which each baraita is true, preserving both as valid rulings in different circumstances - and when a further distinction is proposed, the Gemara's text stops mid-sentence rather than completing it.
learning.resolution: Two resolutions are stated in full: (1) the baraitot reflect a dispute between R. Meir and the Rabbis; (2) both baraitot are the Rabbis, distinguishing a synagogue with a caretaker's residence attached (included) from one without (excluded). A third alternative then begins, proposing both baraitot concern synagogues without a caretaker's residence - but the text is cut off mid-sentence at the physical end of the daf, before stating the distinguishing factor. That third resolution remains unresolved here; the discussion continues on the next daf.

takeaway.text: Not every resolution the Gemara begins reaches a stated conclusion on the same daf. A proposed distinction that is cut off at the daf's physical end must be treated as open, not as a settled ruling - even if a later daf eventually completes it.

reasoningPattern.notes: Two resolutions are completed, each applying a different principle: (1) tanna attribution, (2) caretaker-residence distinction (both Rabbis). A third alternative then opens but the Gemara's text breaks off before stating its content, at the physical end of the daf.

learning.ahaMoment: The second resolution (caretaker vs. no caretaker) is more elegant than the first because it does not require attributing the baraitot to different tannaim - it finds a single factual distinction that reconciles both baraitot as statements of fact rather than conflicting opinions. But even this is not the end: the Gemara immediately proposes a further alternative before the daf runs out.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the second resolution (caretaker vs. no caretaker) is the Gemara's final, settled answer because it is the most refined of the resolutions actually completed. In fact a third alternative begins right after it and is left open, cut off mid-sentence - the sugya does not close on this daf.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two baraitot: synagogues in, synagogues out. Two completed resolutions: R. Meir vs. Rabbis (broadest), caretaker vs. no caretaker (more precise). A third resolution then starts - and the daf cuts off before it says anything. Nothing after that point is settled here.

argumentFlow.label: Contradiction: second baraita excludes synagogues from tzaraat
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: A baraita states: synagogues and study halls are NOT susceptible to tzaraat because they are not designated for one specific person. This contradicts the previous baraita.

sourceRefs.note: The contradicting baraita

argumentFlow.label: Resolution 1: tanna attribution - R. Meir vs. Rabbis
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The first baraita (synagogues included) is R. Meir; the second (synagogues excluded) is the Rabbis. R. Meir's general tendency to include communal structures in personal-ownership categories vs. the Rabbis' stricter reading of 'his house.'

sourceRefs.note: First resolution: attribute to different tannaim

argumentFlow.label: Resolution 2: caretaker's residence vs. none (both baraitot are the Rabbis)
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Alternatively: both baraitot are the Rabbis. A synagogue with a caretaker's residence attached is susceptible to tzaraat (the caretaker = the specific personal owner). One without a caretaker's residence is not susceptible. Both baraitot are factually true in their respective cases.

sourceRefs.note: Second resolution: caretaker-residence distinction

argumentFlow.label: A third alternative begins, cut off mid-sentence at the end of the daf
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara proposes a further alternative: both baraitot concern synagogues WITHOUT a caretaker's residence, distinguished by some other factor instead. The text breaks off mid-sentence - the surviving fragment is 'and the...' - before stating what that factor is. The daf ends here; the resolution is not completed on 11b.

sourceRefs.note: Third resolution begins but is cut off at the physical end of the daf, left unresolved
The terminal fragment 'and the...' at the physical end of the daf

misconceptions.misconception: The caretaker-residence resolution (resolution 2) is the Gemara's final, settled answer to the contradiction.
misconceptions.correction: It is the most refined resolution the Gemara actually completes on this daf, but it is not the end of the discussion. A third alternative begins immediately afterward and is cut off mid-sentence at the physical end of 11b. That third resolution is unresolved here - the sugya continues onto the next daf, and nothing about its eventual content should be read back into 11b.

quizSeeds.question: What resolutions does the Gemara complete for the contradicting baraitot on synagogue tzaraat, and what happens to the resolution it starts after that?
quizSeeds.answer: (1) Tanna attribution: first baraita = R. Meir, second = Rabbis. (2) Both baraitot are the Rabbis, distinguished by whether a caretaker's residence is attached: with caretaker = included, without = excluded. A third alternative then begins but the Gemara's text is cut off mid-sentence at the physical end of the daf, before stating its content - it remains unresolved on 11b.

quizSeeds.question: Why does having a caretaker's residence make a synagogue susceptible to tzaraat, under the second resolution?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the caretaker lives in a residence attached to the synagogue, effectively functioning as the personal owner of the structure. Tzaraat law requires a specific personal owner to receive the divine warning, and the caretaker provides that connection.

glossary.en: A dwelling of honor - one of the conditions for mezuza obligation. Spaces used for undignified purposes (bathrooms, tanneries, bathhouses, mikvaot) fail this test and are exempt from mezuza.

Theoretical completion - R. Meir's principle that if a space could theoretically be carved or enlarged to meet a required minimum measurement, treat it as already meeting that measurement. The Rabbis reject this.

House-plague (tzaraat of a building) - a divine affliction on house walls described in Leviticus 14, requiring personal ownership to apply. For a synagogue, one resolution the Gemara gives ties susceptibility to whether a caretaker's residence is attached; a further distinction is raised but left unresolved at the end of 11b.

The Median gate - a domed arch style of entry (popular in Media/Persia) with no rectangular doorposts. The subject of a dispute between R. Meir (chokkein lehashlem applies, obligated) and the Rabbis (exempt, no real doorposts).

rashiTranslations.en: 'Beit sha'ar' - a small house that they make before the gate of the courtyard, and everyone makes it
a passageway. 'marpeset' - alrod, and it is long, running before the entrances of many upper chambers,
and all of them ascend by way of it. 'achsadra' - a corridor that is before houses. 'a refutation' -
and perforce, the plain case is a Tannaitic dispute. 'and the Median gate' - which they make as a dome, for so they make
in Media. 'that is not roofed' - that it is breached
above completely, without covering. 'and the Sages
exempt' - for there is no gate without a width of four handbreadths,
and every dome narrows at its head to less
than four. 'and they agree that if there is ten at its feet' - before
the curve begins and its width diminishes,
that it is obligated; for even though all is closed from ten
and upward, there is the measure of an opening in its height of ten
by a width of four. 'ten high' - in all. 'and there is not
three at its foot' - the height at which its width diminished
before its height rose three: and it is
nothing' - for anything less than three in height, the earth
is considered packed, and there is no aspect here of the name 'an opening
of four'; and even Rabbi Meir concedes that there is no
beginning here to say 'carve and complete.' 'alternatively, there is
three at its foot' - before its width diminished
from four, and it is not ten high in all, and it is
nothing. 'and there is three at its foot' - in a width
of four, but it is not four wide at its height of ten, for before
it rose ten high its width diminished from four; and there is
room in it to carve and widen the hollow above
to the measure of below; for the wall does not go on,
tapering on the outside according to the inner hollow, like this;
rather, the wall runs long above on the outside
of the hollow, in the proper manner, like this. 'Rabbi Meir holds' -
since it began with three in a width of four, the name
'opening' rests upon it, and we view it as though it were carved
above, widening it to its measure below.
'So that your days be multiplied' - whoever desires life
is implied as obligated. 'the way of your coming' - to the right,
as one comes into the house, and not from the right of one going out. 'for one who
dedicates his house to himself' - that his utensils of use
are designated for himself, and he does not lend them to his neighbors;
that is to say, the plagues come on account of grudging eyes.
This ('of cities') is the catchword anticipating 12a's opening comment.
